analysis.one_liner: Ends the FDA's power to require prescriptions for drugs, except abortion drugs.
analysis.headline: The bill had no cosponsors, never received a committee vote, and died when the 117th Congress ended in January 2023.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would strip the FDA of its authority to require that a drug be dispensed only with a prescription, meaning more medicines could be sold over the counter. It leaves one exception: the government could still require a prescription for drugs used to end a pregnancy. After a six-month waiting period, federal references to prescriptions would be reinterpreted to mean whatever individual state law requires, so states could still impose their own prescription rules.
analysis.who_benefits: Consumers who want to buy medicines without a doctor's visit would get faster, cheaper access, avoiding appointment costs and delays. Generic drug makers and pharmacies could sell a much larger share of their products over the counter, without the prescription gatekeeper.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Consumers avoiding doctor visits, and drug sellers

how_it_helps.text: Repeals the section of the Federal Food, Drug, and Cosmetic Act that gives the FDA authority to require a drug be dispensed only by prescription, effective six months after enactment [S3].
Leaves one exception: the Secretary of Health and Human Services could still require a prescription for any drug intended to terminate a pregnancy [S3].

After the effective date, federal references to prescription drugs would be treated as references to whatever applicable state law requires, so states could still keep or create their own prescription requirements [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Patients who take medicines without medical supervision would bear the safety risk — the prescription requirement exists so a doctor screens for drug interactions, correct dosing, and conditions the drug could harm. Doctors and pharmacists would lose their gatekeeping role over many drugs, and insurers could face shifting costs as more medicines move outside coverage.

drawbacks.text: The prescription system exists because some drugs are dangerous without a doctor's screening; removing it could increase misuse, dangerous drug interactions, and incorrect self-dosing for medicines with narrow safety margins [S2].

The bill's main practical effect would be uncertain: because it converts federal prescription rules to state-law references, each state could keep or restore its own prescription requirements, so access would vary widely by state rather than opening access nationwide [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The upside is real but modest: cheaper, faster access to some medicines for people who cannot easily see a doctor. The downside is a genuine safety risk for drugs that need medical oversight, and the design blunts the benefit anyway by handing the decision back to the states. With no cosponsors and no committee action, the bill was never seriously weighed against those trade-offs.

outcome.mechanism: The bill sat in the House Energy and Commerce Committee and its Health Subcommittee with no cosponsors and no vote, and expired when the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Andy Biggs introduced the bill on January 28, 2022 [S5].
It was referred to the House Committee on Energy and Commerce the same day, and to that committee's Health Subcommittee on January 31, 2022 [S5].
No markup, vote, or further action ever occurred, and the bill died when the 117th Congress ended on January 3, 2023 [S1].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: No concentrated interest gained; the existing system stayed in place, so the FDA kept its authority to require prescriptions and patients kept the safety screening that comes with it.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: No one — the status quo held

for.name: Rep. Andy Biggs
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and filed it in the House [S5].

against.name: Rep. Frank Pallone
against.role: Chair, House Energy and Commerce Committee
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled the bill for a committee markup or vote; it sat in committee until the Congress ended [S5].

sides.party_line_note: No vote was ever taken and no other member cosponsored the bill, including no Republicans, so no partisan split was ever recorded.

industries.note: Removing the federal prescription requirement would open a much larger over-the-counter market, but state-law references leave each state free to restore prescription rules, so the gain is uncertain [S3]. The safety risk to consumers from unsupervised use runs against the public interest even as cheaper access runs with it [S2].

Pharmacies could sell more medicines without a prescription, expanding sales. But the prescription requirement is also what routes customers through pharmacists, so the bill would partly eliminate their gatekeeping role [S3].

Doctors would lose the gatekeeping role and the visits tied to prescribing routine medicines. Patients gain convenience but lose the medical screening that catches dangerous interactions and misuses [S2].
